title: Why the area under a speed–time graph is distance
examples: Why is the area under a speed-time graph the distance?
How far does a car go if it speeds up steadily?
What does integration have to do with area?

marks.label: 10 s: 20 m/s
marks.ask: Why is the area under a speed-time graph the distance?

explain.say: A train leaves a station in Japan and speeds up steadily. This straight line shows its speed, second by second. Look at the yellow mark: at the start, the speed is 0 metres per second.

draw.text: Why the area under a speed–time graph is distance

marks.label: 10 s: 20 m/s
marks.ask: Why is the area under a speed-time graph the distance?

explain.say: First a simpler idea. If you drive at 10 metres per second for 10 seconds, you go 10 times 10, which is 100 metres. On a speed-time graph that is a rectangle, 10 tall and 10 wide. Distance is its area!

marks.label: 10 s: 20 m/s
marks.ask: Why is the area under a speed-time graph the distance?

explain.say: Now look at the purple mark. After 10 seconds the train is at 20 metres per second. The shape under the line is a triangle, 10 wide and 20 tall. Half of 10 times 20 is 100 metres. Do you notice something?

marks.label: 10 s: 20 m/s
marks.ask: Why is the area under a speed-time graph the distance?

explain.say: It is the same 100 metres! Look at the cyan mark: halfway through, the speed is 10. Speeding up steadily from 0 to 20 is like going at 10 the whole time. The area under the line adds up every little bit of distance.

marks.label: 10 s: 20 m/s
marks.ask: Why is the area under a speed-time graph the distance?

explain.say: Well done! Finding the area under a curve is called integration, one of the two big ideas of calculus. Car engineers and space agencies like ISRO use it to work out how far a vehicle has travelled from its speed.

marks.label: 10 s: 20 m/s
marks.ask: Why is the area under a speed-time graph the distance?

faq.q: Why is the area under a speed-time graph the distance?
faq.a: Distance is speed times time. Each thin strip under the graph is a small speed times a small time, so a small distance. Adding all the strips gives the whole distance.
For steady speeding up from 0 to 20 metres per second, the average is halfway, 10 metres per second. Over 10 seconds that gives 100 metres.
asks: What is the average speed when accelerating steadily?

faq.q: How do you find the area of a triangle under the graph?
faq.a: Half times base times height. Here that is half times 10 seconds times 20 metres per second, which is 100 metres.
asks: How do I work out the triangle area?

faq.q: What if the speed-time graph is curved?
faq.a: Then you split the area into thin strips and add them up, or use integration to get the exact area.
asks: How do you find the area under a curved graph?

faq.q: What does the slope of a speed-time graph show?
faq.a: The slope shows acceleration. A slope of 2 means the speed grows by 2 metres per second every second.
asks: What is the gradient of a speed-time graph?

facts: The area under a speed–time graph equals the distance travelled.
Speeding up steadily from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s covers ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m.

quiz.say: A bike goes at a steady 5 m/s for 8 s. How far does it go?
quiz.show: A bike goes at a steady 5 m/s for 8 s. How far does it go?
quiz.why: Distance = speed × time = 5 × 8 = 40 m, the area of the rectangle.

wrong.0: 13 adds speed and time instead of multiplying.

quiz.say: A car speeds up steadily from 0 to 30 m/s in 10 s. How far does it go?
quiz.show: A car speeds up steadily from 0 to 30 m/s in 10 s. How far does it go?
quiz.why: The triangle area is ½ × 10 × 30 = 150 m.

wrong.0: 300 m forgets the half: that is the full rectangle.
wrong.1: 30 is the final speed, not the distance.
